result:
**Construction for n = 12 checks out.** Every assistant starts at 000 at t = 0 and moves outward. Transit assistants leave 000 on a given edge in order of speed, so the faster ones stay ahead and never meet a slower one in an interior point. Each slower bouncer on that edge returns to 000 only after all transits on it have exited. The timings work: for example, assistant 10 crosses 100–110 during [1/1024, 1/512], before assistant 4 reaches 100 at t = 1/16. Each of the 12 edges ends up with exactly one bouncer, and no two bouncers share an edge in steady state.

**The upper bound is not established.** Two bouncers on the same edge with different powers-of-two speeds do cross at an interior point, so each edge holds at most one bouncer. That part is sound. But the argument for n = 13 is hand-waved. A 13th assistant does not have to bounce on an edge; it could pass through bouncer-occupied edges if its arrivals at each vertex are timed exactly with the bouncer's vertex visits. The proposal does not rule this out. The modular "contradiction" $0 \equiv 511 \pmod{1024}$ is asserted without derivation from any actual timing constraint, so it does not support the claim.

I could not construct a configuration with 13 or more assistants, and the answer 12 matches the natural design of the problem (one bouncer per cube edge, and the speeds chosen so transits can be scheduled). So I believe 12 is the intended answer, but the proof of the upper bound is incomplete.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
